mcqs.question: Building a prefix sum array of length n costs how much, and why?
options: O(log n), because each entry can be derived from a binary split of the array
O(n²), because each prefix[i] independently re-sums arr[0..i]
O(n), because each entry adds exactly one new element to the previous running total
O(1), because prefix sums are precomputed at compile time
mcqs.explanation: Each prefix[i] is built as prefix[i-1] + arr[i] — one addition reusing the previous total — so the whole array takes exactly one pass, O(n). Recomputing each entry from scratch would be O(n²), which is exactly what the recurrence avoids.

mcqs.question: Using prefix[r] - prefix[l-1] to answer sum(l, r), what breaks when l = 0?
options: The formula returns 0 incorrectly for any range starting at 0
Nothing breaks — prefix[-1] is defined as 0 by convention in every language
prefix[-1] doesn't exist as a valid array index, forcing a special-case branch
The formula only fails when r also equals 0
mcqs.explanation: There's no prefix[-1] slot in a plain 0-indexed prefix array of length n, so l=0 needs an explicit special case unless you use the sentinel trick. It's not that the result is wrong — the lookup itself is invalid, and no language treats a negative index as an implicit zero by default.

mcqs.question: You need to answer q range-sum queries over a fixed array of size n. When does building a prefix sum first pay off over brute force?
options: Only when q is larger than n²
Almost immediately — the one-time O(n) build plus O(1) per query beats O(n) per query for any non-trivial q
Never — brute force and prefix sums have the same total complexity
Only if the array is sorted first
mcqs.explanation: Brute force costs O(n) per query, O(n·q) total; prefix sums cost O(n) once plus O(1) per query, O(n + q) total — the crossover happens almost immediately once there's more than a handful of queries. Sortedness is irrelevant to either approach.

mcqs.question: Building a 2D prefix sum, why does the recurrence subtract prefix[i-1][j-1]?
options: It's an optimization that isn't strictly necessary for correctness
To handle negative numbers in the matrix
Because 2D prefix sums require normalizing by the diagonal element
To correct for the overlap double-counted by adding both the rectangle above and the rectangle to the left
mcqs.explanation: The rectangle above (i-1,j) and the rectangle to the left (i,j-1) both include the top-left rectangle (i-1,j-1), so adding them both counts that overlap twice; subtracting it once restores the correct total. It's required for correctness, not an optional optimization, and has nothing to do with sign or diagonal normalization.

mcqs.question: To find whether a subarray sums to exactly k in O(n), what does the hash-map-plus-prefix-sum technique look up at each index?
options: Whether the current element itself equals k
Whether an earlier prefix sum equal to (current prefix sum - k) has been seen before
Whether the current prefix sum is a duplicate of any previous prefix sum
Whether k is greater than the maximum element seen so far
mcqs.explanation: If an earlier prefix sum equals the current prefix sum minus k, the subarray between that earlier point and the current index sums to exactly k — so the map is checked for (currentPrefix - k) at every step. Checking for plain duplicate prefix sums or comparing to the current element doesn't answer the actual question being asked.

mcqs.question: The prefix-sum subtraction trick works for sum and XOR. Why doesn't the same trick work for range max?
options: Max has no inverse operation — knowing prefix max over [0,r] and [0,l-1] doesn't let you recover the max of exactly [l,r]
It does work for max, just with division instead of subtraction
Max requires the array to be sorted first, unlike sum or XOR
Max only fails when the array contains negative numbers
mcqs.explanation: Sum and XOR both have an inverse (subtraction, XOR-with-itself) that lets you remove the unwanted prefix; max has no such inverse, since the max of [0,l-1] could equal the max of [l,r] or have nothing to do with it. Range max needs a genuinely different structure like a sparse table, not a tweak to the same formula.
